questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
Other things remaining unchanged, market demand for a good might increase if
1. price of its substitute increases
2. price of its complement increases
3. the good is an inferior good and income of the consumers increases
4. its price falls
Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explain: The amount of a good, service or resource that people are willing and able to buy during a specified period at a specified price is known as the quantity demanded. Statements 1 and 4 are correct: The Demand for a good, service or resource rises if the cost of one of its substitutes rises or if its price falls. Statement 3 is not correct: An inferior good is a term used in economics to describe a product whose demand falls as people's (consumers') earnings rise. Statement 2 is not correct: An object used in combination with another product or service is a complementary good or service. Usually, when consumed alone, the complementary good has little or no value. Still, when paired with another good or service, it adds value to the overall value of the bid. So, if the price of a complement increases, then the other products' demand will decrease.

questions.q: If a commodity is provided free to the public by the Government, then
options: The opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the tax-paying public.
The opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the Government.
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the loss or gain of making a decision. It is the value of what one loses when choosing between two or more options or alternatives. If a commodity is provided free to the public by the Government, then the opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the tax-paying public. The government while providing free commodities to certain consumers uses the tax revenue that it has obtained. The taxpayers could have also availed other benefits out of their paid taxes, hence the opportunity cost of providing a free commodity is in the sense of other prospective benefits that could have been availed, foregone by the tax-paying public.
